claim: Nitrogen is quantitatively the single most limiting nutrient for plants.
source: Quantitatively, nitrogen is the single most limiting nutrient for plants.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction without specific citation.

claim: Maximal crop yield depends critically on nitrogen fertilizer inputs.
source: Thus, not surprisingly, maximal crop yield depends critically on nitrogen fertilizer inputs.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge following from the previous statement about nitrogen limitation.

claim: Current practices require production of approximately 1.5 × 10^7 tons of N-fertilizer per annum.
source: Current practices require production of ∼1.5 × 107 tons of N-fertilizer per annum, consuming ∼1% of the world's annual energy production.
evidence: This is stated as a factual statistic about current fertilizer production.

claim: N-fertilizer production consumes approximately 1% of the world's annual energy production.
source: Current practices require production of ∼1.5 × 107 tons of N-fertilizer per annum, consuming ∼1% of the world's annual energy production.
evidence: This is stated as a factual statistic about energy consumption.

claim: Plants absorb only a fraction of the fertilizer applied to the field.
source: Plants absorb only a fraction of the fertilizer applied to the field, leading to leaching into groundwater, polluting the environment, and damaging human health.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about fertilizer efficiency.

claim: Overexpression of an alanine amino transferase improved nitrogen use efficiency.
source: Overexpression of an alanine amino transferase or the transporter OsPTR9 are two of the few examples of improved nitrogen use efficiency (Shrawat et al., 2008; Fang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Overexpression of the transporter OsPTR9 improved nitrogen use efficiency.
source: Overexpression of an alanine amino transferase or the transporter OsPTR9 are two of the few examples of improved nitrogen use efficiency (Shrawat et al., 2008; Fang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Ammonium, nitrate, amino acids, and di- and tripeptides serve as the major forms of inorganic and organic nitrogen for plants.
source: Ammonium, nitrate, amino acids, and di- and tripeptides serve as the major forms of inorganic and organic nitrogen for plants.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about nitrogen forms.

claim: Nitrogen uptake occurs predominantly from the soil/rhizosphere into roots.
source: Uptake occurs predominantly from the soil/rhizosphere into roots, although aerial parts of the plant are also capable of absorbing nitrogen (McAllister et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Aerial parts of the plant are capable of absorbing nitrogen.
source: Uptake occurs predominantly from the soil/rhizosphere into roots, although aerial parts of the plant are also capable of absorbing nitrogen (McAllister et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Inorganic nitrogen uptake involves multiple ammonium and nitrate uptake systems, typically grouped into low-affinity/high-capacity and high-affinity/low-capacity systems.
source: Inorganic nitrogen uptake is complex and involves multiple ammonium and nitrate uptake systems, typically grouped into low-affinity/high-capacity and high-affinity/low-capacity systems (Siddiqi et al., 1990; Wang et al., 1994; von Wirén et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The 13N-isotope has a short half-life time of approximately 10 minutes.
source: Some studies rely on the analysis of the depletion of the medium, others use stable isotopes, or the 13N-isotope, which has a short half-life time of ∼10 min and requires access to a suitable supply source (Wang et al., 1993; Clarkson et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated as a factual property of the isotope.

claim: Nitrate levels differ dramatically between root cell types.
source: Nitrate levels differ dramatically between root cell types (Zhen et al., 1991; Karley et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The levels of small oligopeptides were comparatively higher in the epidermis and endodermis compared to other root cell types.
source: This study found that the levels of small oligopeptides were comparatively higher in the epidermis and endodermis compared to other root cell types.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a referenced study (Moussaieff et al., 2013).

claim: The nitrate concentration of root vacuoles is approximately 10-fold higher compared to the cytosol.
source: Compartmental analyses indicated that the nitrate concentration of root vacuoles is ∼10-fold higher compared to the cytosol (Zhen et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Three major families of transporters for inorganic nitrogen uptake have been identified: the NPF/POT nitrate transporter family, NRT2 nitrate transporters, and the ammonium transporters of the AMT/MEP/Rh family.
source: Three major families of transporters for inorganic nitrogen uptake (and distribution) have been identified: the NPF/POT nitrate transporter family (Leran et al., 2013), NRT2 nitrate transporters (Kotur et al., 2012), and the ammonium transporters of the AMT/MEP/Rh family (von Wirén et al., 2000; Andrade and Einsle, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Members of the NPF/POT family play important roles in the transport of histidine, dicarboxylates, oligopeptides, and glucosinolates.
source: In addition to their role in nitrate uptake, members of the NPF/POT (Leran et al., 2013) family play important roles also in the transport of histidine, dicarboxylates, oligopeptides, and glucosinolates, and surprisingly at least three major plant hormones: auxin, ABA, and gibberellin (Krouk et al., 2010; Kanno et al., 2012; Boursiac et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: At least three major plant hormones (auxin, ABA, and gibberellin) are transported by members of the NPF/POT family.
source: In addition to their role in nitrate uptake, members of the NPF/POT (Leran et al., 2013) family play important roles also in the transport of histidine, dicarboxylates, oligopeptides, and glucosinolates, and surprisingly at least three major plant hormones: auxin, ABA, and gibberellin (Krouk et al., 2010; Kanno et al., 2012; Boursiac et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The majority of changes in nitrate-induced gene expression are cell-specific.
source: Analysis of cell type-specific expression profiles showed that the majority of changes in nitrate-induced gene expression are cell-specific (Gifford et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Nitrate transporters are regulated through phosphorylation, mediated by calcium-dependent calcineurin-like kinases (CBL and CIPK).
source: Nitrate transporters are regulated through phosphorylation, mediated by calcium-dependent calcineurin-like kinases (Calcineurin B-like, CBL and CBL-interacting protein kinase, CIPK) (Ho et al., 2009; Hu et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Members of the AMT and NPF/POT family function as transporters and receptors (transceptors).
source: Major breakthroughs were findings that indicate both the members of the AMT and NPF/POT family function as transporters and receptors (transceptors) (Ho et al., 2009; Lima et al., 2010; Rubio-Texeira et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Many transporters undergo conformational changes during the transport cycle.
source: Biochemical and structural analyses have shown that many transporters undergo conformational changes during the transport cycle (Shimamura et al., 2010; Jiang, 2012a; Krishnamurthy and Gouaux, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Conformational rearrangements have been observed for many members of the MFS superfamily, including members of the NPF/POT family.
source: Important in this context is that such rearrangements have been observed for many members of the MFS superfamily, including members of the NPF/POT family (Doki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: AmTrac uses ammonium transporters as sensory domains by inserting a circularly permutated EGFP into a conformation-sensitive position.
source: The first prototype for transport activity sensors, named AmTrac, uses ammonium transporters as sensory domains for engineering transport activity sensors by inserting a circularly permutated EGFP (cpEGFP) into a conformation-sensitive position of an ammonium transporter (De Michele et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Addition of ammonium to yeast cells expressing the AmTrac sensor triggers concentration-dependent and reversible changes in fluorescence intensity.
source: Addition of ammonium to yeast cells expressing the AmTrac sensor triggers concentration-dependent and reversible changes in fluorescence intensity (De Michele et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: NiTrac1 was created by sandwiching CHL1 between a yellow acceptor (Aphrodite) and cyan donor fluorophore (mCerulean).
source: It is likely that the nitrate transceptor CHL1 undergoes conformational rearrangements during its transport cycle. To measure substrate-dependent conformational rearrangements, CHL1 was sandwiched between a yellow acceptor (Aphrodite) and cyan donor fluorophore (mCerulean) (Rizzo et al., 2006; Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for creating NiTrac1, with reference to Figure 1A showing the construct.

claim: Addition of nitrate to yeast expressing NiTrac1 triggered an overall reduction in the emission intensities of both donor and acceptor.
source: To our surprise, and in contrast to typical FRET sensors (e.g., glucose or glutamate [Fehr et al., 2003; Okumoto et al., 2005]), we observed an overall reduction in the emission intensities of both donor and acceptor, but no obvious change in FRET efficiency.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Aphrodite emission was unaffected by nitrate when excited directly.
source: However, Aphrodite emission was unaffected by nitrate when excited directly (Figure 1B, inset), indicating that the external nitrate triggers donor quenching in the cytosol.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B inset.

claim: External nitrate triggers donor quenching in the cytosol.
source: However, Aphrodite emission was unaffected by nitrate when excited directly (Figure 1B, inset), indicating that the external nitrate triggers donor quenching in the cytosol.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Aphrodite emission is unaffected when excited directly.

claim: The nitrate analog chlorate triggered NiTrac quenching.
source: As one may have expected, the nitrate analog chlorate that lead to the naming of CHL1 (chlorate resistance of the chl1 mutant) (Tsay, 1993) also triggered NiTrac quenching (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The response of NiTrac1 is nitrate- and chlorate-specific; other compounds such as chloride, ammonium, divalent cations, and dipeptide had no significant effect.
source: The response of NiTrac1 is nitrate- and chlorate-specific; other compounds such as chloride, ammonium, divalent cations, and dipeptide had no significant effect (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: When mCerulean was replaced by mTFP, nitrate addition had no effect on the emission of the NiTrac1 variant.
source: When mCerulean was replaced by the corral-derived cyan fluorescent protein mTFP (Ai et al., 2008), we observed FRET, but nitrate addition had no effect on the emission of this variant (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Replacement of mCerulean with eCFP retained the donor-quenching response to nitrate.
source: Replacement of mCerulean with eCFP, another jellyfish variant, retained the donor-quenching response to nitrate (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Addition of nitrate to yeast cells expressing CHL1 alone had no effect on the fluorescence of a cytosolically expressed mCerulean.
source: However, addition of nitrate to yeast cells expressing CHL1 alone had no effect on the fluorescence of a cytosolically expressed mCerulean (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: PepTrac1, PepTrac2, and PepTrac5 sensors all responded with donor quenching to the addition of 0.5 mM diglycine.
source: PepTrac1, PepTrac2, and PepTrac5 sensors all responded with donor quenching to the addition of 0.5 mM diglycine (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 2B-D.

claim: PepTrac4 responded to substrate addition with a ratio change that is consistent with a change in the energy transfer rate rather than donor quenching.
source: Interestingly, PepTrac4 responded to substrate addition with a ratio change that is consistent with a change in the energy transfer rate rather than donor quenching (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CHL1 shows biphasic nitrate uptake kinetics.
source: CHL1 is unusual in that it shows biphasic nitrate uptake kinetics (Figure 3A; Liu and Tsay, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by both experimental data in Figure 3A and a citation to published research.

claim: The kinetics of the fluorescence response of NiTrac1 in yeast were biphasic.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the kinetics of the fluorescence response of NiTrac1 in yeast were also biphasic (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mutation of T101 to alanine eliminated the high-affinity component of CHL1.
source: Mutation of T101 to alanine had been shown to eliminate the high-affinity component (Figure 3B; Liu and Tsay, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by both experimental data in Figure 3B and a citation to published research.

claim: Introduction of T101A into NiTrac1 eliminated the high-affinity component.
source: Introduction of T101A into NiTrac1 also eliminated the high-affinity component, intimating that NiTrac1 is a transport activity sensor, and that conformational rearrangements during the transport cycle affect mCerulean emission (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The transport Kms of both high- and low-affinity phases matched the values obtained for the fluorescence response.
source: Interestingly, the transport Kms of both high- and low-affinity phases matched the values obtained for the fluorescence response, supporting the hypothesis that NiTrac measures the transport activity.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the kinetic data from transport and fluorescence measurements.

claim: The sensor can be used effectively for in planta analyses based on rapid nitrate-induced quenching and reversibility in individual yeast cells.
source: Measurement of the sensor response in individual yeast cells demonstrated rapid nitrate-induced quenching and reversibility of the fluorescence intensity after removal of nitrate (Figure 3C), indicating that the sensor can be used effectively for in planta analyses.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 3C demonstrating reversibility.

claim: The Kms of NiTrac1 for nitrate are approximately 75.1 ± 21 μM and 3.8 ± 2.6 mM.
source: The Kms of NiTrac1 for nitrate are ∼75.1 ± 21 μM and 3.8 ± 2.6 mM; for NiTrac1-T101A is 3.5 ± 3.7 mM.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The Km of NiTrac1-T101A for nitrate is 3.5 ± 3.7 mM.
source: The Kms of NiTrac1 for nitrate are ∼75.1 ± 21 μM and 3.8 ± 2.6 mM; for NiTrac1-T101A is 3.5 ± 3.7 mM.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data.

claim: CHL1 contains a highly conserved motif E41-E44-R45 in TM1 predicted to play a role in proton coupling.
source: CHL1 contains a highly conserved motif E41-E44-R45 in TM1 predicted to play a role in proton coupling (Newstead, 2011; Newstead et al., 2011; Solcan et al., 2012; Doki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on structural predictions and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Mutations in the E41-E44-R45 motif in oligopeptide transporters typically lost proton-driven transport activity.
source: Mutations in this motif in the oligopeptide transporters PepTSt (from Streptococcus thermophiles [Solcan et al., 2012]), PepTSo, PepTSo2 (both from Shewanella oneidensis) (Newstead, 2011), and GkPOT (from Geobacillus kaustophilus) (Doki et al., 2013) typically lost proton-driven transport activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on bacterial transporters.

claim: Mutation in any of the three residues (E41A, E44A, and R45A, TM1) led to a loss of nitrate-induced currents and 15N-uptake in both the high- and low-affinity range.
source: Mutation in any of the three residues (E41A, E44A, and R45A, TM1) led to a loss of nitrate-induced currents and 15N-uptake in both the high- and low-affinity range (0.5/0.25 and 10 mM) (Figures 5, 6).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The corresponding mutant of NiTrac1 (E41A, E44A, or R45A) lost the sensor response to nitrate addition.
source: The corresponding mutant of NiTrac1 also lost the sensor response to nitrate addition (Figures 4B, 7), indicating that the conserved motif is also used for proton cotransport of nitrate.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 4B and 7.

claim: The conserved motif E41-E44-R45 is used for proton cotransport of nitrate.
source: The corresponding mutant of NiTrac1 also lost the sensor response to nitrate addition (Figures 4B, 7), indicating that the conserved motif is also used for proton cotransport of nitrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of function in mutants affecting this motif.

claim: A salt bridge between K126 in TM4 and E400 in TM10 is implicated in peptide recognition and/or structural movements during the transport cycle in PepTSt.
source: Structural and functional analyses of the bacterial peptide transporter PepTSt had implicated a salt bridge between a conserved K126 in TM4 and E400 in TM10 in peptide recognition and/or structural movements during the transport cycle (Solcan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: K164 in CHL1 is conserved throughout the POT family.
source: This lysine is conserved throughout the POT family (K164 of CHL1, TM4) (Newstead, 2011; Newstead et al., 2011; Solcan et al., 2012; Doki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on sequence conservation.

claim: Mutation of K164 to alanine or aspartate in CHL1 completely abolished nitrate uptake in both the high- and low-affinity range.
source: Consistent with results from the bacterial PepTSt and GkPOT, mutation of K164 to alanine or aspartate in CHL1 completely abolished nitrate uptake in both the high- and low-affinity range (0.25 and 10 mM) (Figure 6); however, the nitrate-dependent inward currents were retained (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: CHL1-K164 mutants retained nitrate-dependent inward currents despite loss of uptake.
source: Consistent with results from the bacterial PepTSt and GkPOT, mutation of K164 to alanine or aspartate in CHL1 completely abolished nitrate uptake in both the high- and low-affinity range (0.25 and 10 mM) (Figure 6); however, the nitrate-dependent inward currents were retained (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: CHL1-K164 mutants either function as nitrate-dependent proton channels or have lost selectivity.
source: Both CHL1-K164 mutants either function as nitrate-dependent proton channels or have lost selectivity, and consistent with the shift of the reversal potential to more negative values transport other anions such as chloride.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation of retained currents but lost uptake.

claim: NiTrac1-K164A showed both donor quenching and a change in FRET efficiency upon addition of nitrate.
source: NiTrac1-K164A surprisingly showed a different response mode, that is upon addition of nitrate the mutant not only showed donor quenching but apparently also a change in FRET efficiency, underlining the exceptional sensitivity of NiTrac1 to effects of mutations on conformation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mutation of E476A in TM10 of CHL1 led to loss of both the nitrate-induced inward current and 15N-uptake.
source: Mutation of the salt bridge acceptor E476A in TM10 of CHL1 led to loss of both the nitrate-induced inward current and 15N-uptake (Figures 5, 6) and NiTrac lost the sensor response to addition of nitrate (Figure 4B);
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 4B, 5, and 6.

claim: The conservative mutation E476D had no significant effect on transport properties and sensor response.
source: by contrast, and as one might expect, the conservative mutation E476D had no significant effect on transport properties and sensor response (Figures 4B, 5, and 6).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 4B, 5, and 6.

claim: Y388A had no detectable effect on the nitrate-induced inward currents, 15N-uptake, and sensor response.
source: Consistent with the results obtained for the corresponding residue (N342 in TM8) in GKPOT (Doki et al., 2013), Y388A had no detectable effect on the nitrate-induced inward currents, 15N-uptake, and sensor response (Figures 4B, 5, and 6), indicating the residue Y388 may not be involved in nitrate binding or transport cycle of CHL1.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 4B, 5, and 6.

claim: The residue Y388 may not be involved in nitrate binding or transport cycle of CHL1.
source: Consistent with the results obtained for the corresponding residue (N342 in TM8) in GKPOT (Doki et al., 2013), Y388A had no detectable effect on the nitrate-induced inward currents, 15N-uptake, and sensor response (Figures 4B, 5, and 6), indicating the residue Y388 may not be involved in nitrate binding or transport cycle of CHL1.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of the Y388A mutation.

claim: Mutation of L49 in TM1 and Q358 in TM7 of CHL1 to alanine had no significant effect on nitrate-induced inward currents and 15N-uptake.
source: Mutation of L49 in TM1 and Q358 in TM7 of CHL1 to alanine had no significant effect on nitrate-induced inward currents and 15N-uptake (Figures 5, 6), but NiTrac responses were characterized by a mixture of donor quenching and FRET change (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 4B, 5, and 6.

claim: The corresponding NiTrac1 triple mutant (E264A-E266A-K267A) lost the sensor response to high nitrate concentrations.
source: Similarly, the corresponding NiTrac1 mutant also lost the sensor response to high nitrate concentrations (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CIPK23 can phosphorylate CHL1 at T101 in in vitro assays.
source: Therefore, we tested whether coexpression of the known interactor CIPK23, which can phosphorylate CHL1 at T101 in in vitro assays, would affect the properties of NiTrac1 (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated as known information, likely from previous studies.

claim: CIPK23 did not change the energy transfer between the fluorophores in the absence of nitrate.
source: CIPK23 did not change the energy transfer between the fluorophores in the absence of nitrate, but blocked the fluorescence response of NiTrac1 to nitrate addition (Figure 8B), either by stoichiometric binding or by phosphorylation of T101.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: CIPK23 blocked the fluorescence response of NiTrac1 to nitrate addition.
source: CIPK23 did not change the energy transfer between the fluorophores in the absence of nitrate, but blocked the fluorescence response of NiTrac1 to nitrate addition (Figure 8B), either by stoichiometric binding or by phosphorylation of T101.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: CBL9 enhanced the CIPK23-mediated phosphorylation of CHL1.
source: The coactivator CBL9, which did not affect CHL1 transport activity on its own but enhanced the CIPK23-mediated phosphorylation of CHL1 (Ho et al., 2009), had no detectable effect on the fluorescence response of NiTrac1 by itself (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: CBL9 had no detectable effect on the fluorescence response of NiTrac1 by itself.
source: The coactivator CBL9, which did not affect CHL1 transport activity on its own but enhanced the CIPK23-mediated phosphorylation of CHL1 (Ho et al., 2009), had no detectable effect on the fluorescence response of NiTrac1 by itself (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: CIPK8 is nitrate inducible in a CHL1-dependent fashion.
source: By contrast, CIPK8, which is nitrate inducible in a CHL1-dependent fashion, did not affect the Nitrac1 response.
evidence: This is stated as known information, likely from previous studies.

claim: CIPK8 did not affect the NiTrac1 response.
source: By contrast, CIPK8, which is nitrate inducible in a CHL1-dependent fashion, did not affect the Nitrac1 response.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: CBL1 blocked the NiTrac1 response to nitrate addition.
source: However, CBL1 on its own also blocked the Nitrac1 response to nitrate addition (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The potassium transporter KT2 blocked NiTrac1 responses.
source: Although two of the four did not show significant effects on NiTrac1 or the response to nitrate addition, we found that the potassium transporter KT2 and the WNK kinase WNK8 blocked NiTrac1 responses (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The WNK kinase WNK8 blocked NiTrac1 responses.
source: Although two of the four did not show significant effects on NiTrac1 or the response to nitrate addition, we found that the potassium transporter KT2 and the WNK kinase WNK8 blocked NiTrac1 responses (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The most striking feature of NiTrac is the biphasic response kinetic that matches the dual-affinity transport properties of the protein.
source: The most striking feature of NiTrac is the biphasic response kinetic that matches the dual-affinity transport properties of the protein strikingly well.
evidence: This is a summary observation comparing the sensor response to transport kinetics.

claim: NiTrac1 is a sensitive tool for reporting conformational changes in mutants.
source: Together, these data show that NiTrac1 is a sensitive tool for reporting conformational changes in mutants and further support the hypothesis that NiTrac1 reports activity states of the transporter.
evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive mutational analysis data.

claim: NiTrac1 reports activity states of the transporter.
source: Together, these data show that NiTrac1 is a sensitive tool for reporting conformational changes in mutants and further support the hypothesis that NiTrac1 reports activity states of the transporter.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between transport activity and sensor output.

claim: The dual-affinity of CHL1 is not caused by partial phosphorylation when expressed in oocytes but represents an intrinsic property of CHL1.
source: These findings strongly supported the notion that NiTrac reports the processes that occur in the transceptor, when it binds and/or transports nitrate. The observations also intimate that the dual-affinity is not caused by partial phosphorylation of CHL1 when expressed in oocytes, as suggested by Tsay's group (Liu and Tsay, 2003), but more likely represent an intrinsic property of CHL1 since they also occur when NiTrac1 is expressed in yeast.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that biphasic kinetics occur in yeast, which is unlikely to phosphorylate the transporter.

claim: CHL1 functions as nitrate sensor to regulate transcription of a variety of genes including that of the high-affinity nitrate transporter NRT2.
source: CHL1 also functions as nitrate sensor to regulate transcription of a variety of genes including that of the high-affinity nitrate transporter NRT2 (Ho et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The transport and signaling activities of CHL1 can be decoupled by Pro492L mutation in the loop connecting TM10 and 11.
source: Interestingly, the transport and signaling activities of CHL1 can be decoupled by Pro492L in the loop connecting TM10 and 11 (Ho et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Activity sensors can be used to probe protein interactions with exquisite sensitivity.
source: The interaction of proteins likely affects the conformation of both partners, either directly or as a consequence of modifications such as phosphorylation. Here we show that activity sensors can be used to probe such interactions with exquisite sensitivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful demonstration of detecting regulatory protein effects on NiTrac1.

claim: CIPK23 can interact with CHL1 on its own and trigger at least partial phosphorylation of T101 in vitro.
source: Although typically CIPKs are thought to require a CBL for substrate recognition and derepression of the autoinhibition, CIPK23 had been shown to be able to interact with CHL1 on its own and trigger at least partial phosphorylation of T101 in vitro (Ho et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: CBL9 enhanced the CIPK-mediated phosphorylation of T101.
source: Interestingly, although CBL9 had been shown to enhance the CIPK-mediated phosphorylation of T101, we did not observe an effect of coexpression of CBL on NiTrac1.
evidence: This is stated as known information from previous studies.

claim: AtCBL1 and AtCBL9 share approximately 89% identity.
source: Surprisingly, and despite the high sequence identity between AtCBL9 and AtCBL1 (∼89% identity), CBL1 but not CBL9 inhibited the nitrate response of NiTrac1.
evidence: This is stated as a factual observation about sequence identity.

claim: AtCBL1 and 9 have been shown to regulate a variety of processes including potassium uptake, pollen germination, as well as sugar-, hormone- and ROS-signaling.
source: AtCBL1 and 9 have been shown to regulate a variety of processes including potassium uptake, pollen germination, as well as sugar-, hormone- and ROS-signaling (Sagi and Fluhr, 2006; Xu et al., 2006; Cheong et al., 2007; Hashimoto and Kudla, 2011; Drerup et al., 2013; Kimura et al., 2013; Li, 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The AtCBL1-AtCIPK1 complex is involved in ABA-dependent stress responses.
source: Even though CBL1 and 9 have apparent overlapping functions, they can have specific effects, for example, the AtCBL1-AtCIPK1 complex is involved in ABA-dependent stress responses, whereas the AtCBL9-AtCIPK1 complex plays roles in ABA-independent stress responses (Drerup et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The AtCBL9-AtCIPK1 complex plays roles in ABA-independent stress responses.
source: Even though CBL1 and 9 have apparent overlapping functions, they can have specific effects, for example, the AtCBL1-AtCIPK1 complex is involved in ABA-dependent stress responses, whereas the AtCBL9-AtCIPK1 complex plays roles in ABA-independent stress responses (Drerup et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Full-length CIPK23, CIPK16, or CIPK6 alone can activate the AKT1 potassium channel system.
source: However, recent studies showed that full-length CIPK23, CIPK16, or CIPK6 alone can activate the AKT1 potassium channel system (Li et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2007; Fujii et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: AtCBL10 interacts with AKT1 to regulate potassium homeostasis without binding to any AtCIPKs.
source: Also, AtCBL10 interacts with AKT1 to regulate potassium homeostasis without binding to any AtCIPKs (Ren et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: AtKT2/KUP2/SHY3 plays a role in potassium uptake.
